title: Birthday money
description: Decide how to use a birthday gift wisely.
preview: You receive birthday money and need to think about spending, saving, and what matters most to you.
cubHint: Consider what you want now and what you might wish you still had later.
situation: You receive Rs. 5,000 as birthday money. Nothing is owed today. A bigger goal you have mentioned would cost about Rs. 8,000.

facts.label: Due date
facts.value: No fixed deadline in this scenario

options.title: Spend the gift now
options.summary: Use the birthday money on something you want today.
bullets: Nothing is left from this gift.
You do not take on debt.
options.immediate: You enjoy the gift immediately and have Rs. 0 left from it.
options.future: A later goal would need new money, because this gift would already be spent.

snapshot.label: Spend now
snapshot.note: No debt. The Rs. 5,000 gift is gone unless you earn or receive more.

options.title: Save most and spend a little
options.summary: Keep most of the gift and use a small part now.
bullets: You still need about Rs. 4,000 more for the example Rs. 8,000 goal.
options.immediate: You enjoy a small treat and still have Rs. 4,000 set aside.
options.future: The remaining money can go toward a goal, but it does not cover an Rs. 8,000 goal by itself.

snapshot.label: Split the gift
snapshot.note: No debt. The example goal is still short by about Rs. 4,000.

options.title: Save the full gift
options.summary: Put all of the birthday money toward a later goal.
bullets: You avoid debt, and the example goal is still short by Rs. 3,000.
options.immediate: You keep Rs. 5,000 and do not buy something with the gift today.
options.future: Waiting protects the money, but you give up using it for something you might want now.

snapshot.label: Save the gift
snapshot.note: No debt. About Rs. 3,000 more would still be needed for the example goal.

sixMonthAssumptions: This comparison is a teaching sketch, not a prediction of your real life.
No interest or extra fees are added, because none are stated in the scenario.
Spending the gift now assumes you do not replace that money later.
None of these paths is labelled as the only correct choice.
waitAssumption: The Rs. 8,000 goal is a scenario example so you can compare spending now with saving. It is not a required purchase.

title: Friend wants a loan
description: Think about lending money to a friend.
preview: A friend asks to borrow money. Think about trust, repayment, and how it might affect your friendship.
cubHint: Lending is a choice about money and about people. Both matter.
situation: You have Rs. 3,000 saved. A friend asks to borrow Rs. 2,000 and says they will repay you next month.

facts.label: What you would keep if you lend it all
Repayment promise
facts.value: Next month — a promise, not a guarantee

options.title: Lend the full Rs. 2,000
options.summary: Help your friend with the full amount they asked for.
bullets: You are relying on their promise to repay.
options.immediate: Your friend has the money, and your savings drop to Rs. 1,000.
options.future: If repayment is late or does not happen, you may not be able to use that Rs. 2,000 yourself.

snapshot.label: Lend it all
snapshot.note: You do not owe anyone. The Rs. 2,000 is with your friend and is not guaranteed to return.

options.title: Lend a smaller amount
options.summary: Offer Rs. 800, which leaves most of your savings intact.
bullets: Be clear that this is the amount you can offer.
options.immediate: You help with part of the request and keep Rs. 2,200.
options.future: Your friend may still need more money. The Rs. 800 is also not guaranteed to come back.

snapshot.label: Lend less
snapshot.note: You do not owe anyone. Only Rs. 800 is at risk if repayment does not happen.

options.title: Do not lend the money
options.summary: Keep your savings and offer a kind of help that is not cash.
bullets: Explain that you cannot lend it.
You could still help in another way, such as planning or company.
options.immediate: Your savings stay at Rs. 3,000, and your friend does not receive the loan.
options.future: You avoid the repayment risk. Your friend may feel disappointed, so how you explain it matters.

snapshot.label: Do not lend
snapshot.note: Savings stay with you. This choice can still affect the friendship.

sixMonthAssumptions: This comparison is a teaching sketch, not a prediction of your friendship or your finances.
Lent money is not shown as returned, because no repayment has actually happened.
Saying no keeps your savings, and it can still affect how your friend feels.
None of these paths is labelled as the only correct choice.
waitAssumption: “Next month” is what your friend said. This scenario does not prove the money will come back.

title: Buy now, pay later
description: Explore spending now and paying later.
preview: An offer lets you take something home today and pay over time. What is the trade-off?
cubHint: Paying later can feel easy now. Ask what you will still owe.
situation: You have Rs. 3,000 saved. Headphones you want cost Rs. 8,000. A buy-now-pay-later offer asks for Rs. 2,000 today and then Rs. 2,200 three more times.

facts.label: Full price if you pay once
Pay-later total
facts.value: Rs. 8,600 (Rs. 600 more than the cash price)

options.title: Use buy now, pay later
options.summary: Take the headphones today and owe the later payments.
options.immediate: You get the headphones now, with Rs. 6,600 still to pay.
options.future: Those later payments continue even if you want to spend the money on something else.

snapshot.label: Pay later
snapshot.note: Rs. 6,600 stays owed until a real payment schedule is completed.

options.title: Wait and pay the full price
options.summary: Do not take the offer. Save until you can pay Rs. 8,000.
bullets: Do not start the pay-later plan.
You still need Rs. 5,000 more before you can pay the cash price.
options.immediate: You do not get the headphones today, and you do not owe a payment plan.
options.future: Waiting avoids the extra Rs. 600, but you have to manage without the headphones until you can pay.

snapshot.label: Wait
snapshot.note: No debt. You are still Rs. 5,000 short of the Rs. 8,000 cash price.

options.title: Buy a cheaper pair now
options.summary: Choose headphones that cost Rs. 2,500 and pay in full.
bullets: You do not join the payment plan.
options.immediate: You get a cheaper pair and keep Rs. 500, with nothing left to pay.
options.future: You avoid later payments. The cheaper pair may not be the one you wanted most.

snapshot.label: Cheaper pair
snapshot.note: No debt. This uses an example price of Rs. 2,500.

sixMonthAssumptions: This comparison is a teaching sketch, not a shop quote.
The pay-later path still shows Rs. 6,600 owing if no later payments are defined.
Waiting assumes you do not get the headphones today.
The cheaper pair is an example product at Rs. 2,500, not a real listing.
None of these paths is labelled as the only correct choice.
waitAssumption: The extra Rs. 600 and the three later payments are assumptions for this offer. A real offer could differ.

title: Tuition and a festival
preview: School costs and a festival are both coming up. How do you balance learning and enjoyment?
cubHint: Needs and celebrations can both be important. Plan for both if you can.
situation: You have Rs. 5,000. School tuition of Rs. 4,500 is due soon. A festival with friends would cost about Rs. 2,000.

options.title: Pay tuition and skip the festival
options.summary: Cover the school cost and do not spend on the festival.
options.immediate: Tuition is covered and you have Rs. 500 left.
options.future: You miss the festival. You do not leave a school bill unpaid.

snapshot.label: Tuition first
snapshot.note: Nothing is left owing for tuition in this path.

options.title: Go to the festival and pay only part of tuition
options.summary: Spend Rs. 2,000 on the festival and put Rs. 3,000 toward tuition.
bullets: Spend about Rs. 2,000 on the festival.
Rs. 1,500 of tuition is still unpaid.
options.immediate: You can join the festival, but Rs. 1,500 of tuition is still due.
options.future: You will need a plan for the remaining tuition. This scenario does not add a late fee.

snapshot.label: Festival first
snapshot.note: Rs. 1,500 of tuition is still due. No late fee is included because none was stated.

options.title: Pay tuition and use a small festival budget
options.summary: Pay the school cost and keep the celebration much smaller.
bullets: Use Rs. 300 of the remainder for a small festival plan.
options.immediate: Tuition is covered, and you still have a small way to join in.
options.future: The smaller plan may not match everything your friends are doing. The school cost is handled.

snapshot.label: Small budget
snapshot.state: Tuition paid, small festival budget used
snapshot.note: The Rs. 300 festival budget is an example, not a ticket price.

sixMonthAssumptions: This comparison is a teaching sketch, not a school bill.
Any tuition still unpaid is shown as still due, because no later payment is defined.
The festival is treated as optional enjoyment, not as a school requirement.
None of these paths is labelled as the only correct choice.
waitAssumption: The festival cost is an example. The scenario does not include a fine for late tuition, because no fine was stated.

title: The phone that broke
description: Repair, borrow to buy new, or wait and save.
preview: Your phone is broken and you need to decide what to do. Should you repair it, borrow money to buy a new one, or wait and save?
cubHint: Consider what you need now, what you may need later, and the trade-offs of each option.
situation: You have Rs. 6,000 saved. Your phone has broken, and you need to decide what to do.

facts.label: Cousin offer
facts.value: Willing to lend the extra money to buy a new phone

options.title: Borrow and buy a new phone
options.summary: Use your savings and borrow the rest from your cousin.
options.immediate: You get a new phone, but you owe your cousin Rs. 14,000.
options.future: You need to plan how and when to repay the loan, while still covering other needs.

snapshot.label: Borrow and buy
snapshot.note: Savings are used. Rs. 14,000 is still owed unless a repayment plan is defined.

options.title: Repair your current phone
options.summary: Pay for a repair and keep some savings.
bullets: Continue using your repaired phone without taking on new debt.
options.immediate: You spend Rs. 4,000 and retain Rs. 2,000 in savings.
options.future: You avoid new borrowing and can continue using your current phone, assuming the repair works.

snapshot.label: Repair
snapshot.note: No new borrowing. You have Rs. 2,000 left.

options.title: Wait and save
options.summary: Keep your savings and wait until you can buy a new phone.
bullets: Continue saving until you can afford the new phone.
Avoid borrowing money for the purchase.
options.immediate: You delay getting a new phone and retain your savings while planning for the purchase.
options.future: Waiting can help you avoid debt, but you must consider whether you can manage without a working phone in the meantime.

snapshot.label: Wait and save
snapshot.note: Savings stay at Rs. 6,000. A new phone is still unaffordable today.

sixMonthAssumptions: This comparison is a teaching sketch, not a prediction of your real life.
No repayment schedule is defined, so borrowed money is shown as still owing unless you said how you would repay it.
The repair path assumes the repair continues to work for six months.
The wait-and-save path uses the 14-week saving example only as an assumption (about Rs. 1,000 a week).
None of these paths is labelled as the only correct choice.
waitAssumption: If you wait and save Rs. 1,000 a week, it would take about 14 weeks to cover the remaining Rs. 14,000. That waiting time is a scenario assumption, not a guaranteed result.

title: First salary
description: Plan how to divide income between needs and goals.
preview: Your first salary arrives. How might you divide it between needs, saving, and goals?
cubHint: A plan for income often starts with needs, then goals, then wants.
situation: Your first salary is Rs. 12,000. About Rs. 6,000 covers needs such as transport and food. You also want to save for a short course.

facts.label: Course goal
facts.value: Not priced in this scenario — you choose how much to set aside

options.title: Cover needs, then spend the rest
options.summary: Pay for needs and use what remains on things you want.
bullets: Nothing is set aside for the course.
options.immediate: Needs are covered and you can enjoy the rest of the salary.
options.future: The course goal does not move forward with this month’s pay.

snapshot.label: Spend the rest
snapshot.note: No debt. The course goal gets Rs. 0 from this salary.

options.title: Cover needs, save, then wants
options.summary: Set aside Rs. 3,000 after needs and keep Rs. 3,000 for wants.
options.immediate: Needs, a saving goal, and some spending all have a share.
options.future: The course gets Rs. 3,000 this month. You have less free spending than option A.

snapshot.label: Plan the split
snapshot.note: No debt. Wants are limited to about Rs. 3,000 in this example.

options.title: Save aggressively
options.summary: Cut spending hard so you can save Rs. 7,000.
bullets: This assumes you can safely spend less than the Rs. 6,000 needs estimate.
options.immediate: You save a large amount, if the lower spending is actually possible.
options.future: The course grows faster, but cutting needs can be difficult or unwise if the estimate was realistic.

snapshot.label: Save most
snapshot.state: Rs. 7,000 saved, spending cut to Rs. 5,000
snapshot.note: This path assumes you can live on less than the Rs. 6,000 needs estimate.

sixMonthAssumptions: This comparison looks at one salary, not six months of income.
No tax, rent, or course price is added, because those amounts are not given.
Cutting needs below Rs. 6,000 is an assumption and may not be realistic.
None of these paths is labelled as the only correct choice.
waitAssumption: The Rs. 6,000 needs figure is an estimate for this month. Real needs can be higher or lower.

title: Lending to family
description: Evaluate a request for financial help.
preview: A family member asks for financial help. Think about what you can offer and what you cannot.
cubHint: Helping family can be kind. It still needs a clear limit you can afford.
situation: You have Rs. 10,000 saved for a school trip that costs Rs. 7,500. A family member asks for Rs. 8,000 in help.

facts.label: Spare if the trip is kept

options.title: Give the Rs. 8,000
options.summary: Provide the full amount your family member asked for.
bullets: The Rs. 7,500 trip is no longer covered.
options.immediate: Your family member receives the help, and the trip fund is short.
options.future: You would need Rs. 5,500 more to afford the trip. Getting the Rs. 8,000 back is not promised.

snapshot.label: Give it
snapshot.note: You do not owe a lender. The trip is short by Rs. 5,500, and the gift is not shown as repaid.

options.title: Offer Rs. 1,500 you can spare
options.summary: Help with an amount that still leaves the trip covered.
bullets: The trip still fits, with Rs. 1,000 left over.
options.immediate: You help within a limit and can still pay for the trip.
options.future: Your family member may need more than Rs. 1,500. Say clearly whether this money is a gift or a loan.

snapshot.label: Offer a limit
snapshot.note: Rs. 1,500 is no longer in your savings. Repayment is not assumed.

options.title: Do not give the money
options.summary: Protect the trip savings and offer help that is not cash.
options.immediate: The trip fund stays intact, and no cash help is given.
options.future: The family request is unanswered in money terms. Your explanation still matters.

snapshot.label: Keep the fund
snapshot.note: The trip remains affordable. This choice can still be hard to say.

sixMonthAssumptions: This comparison is a teaching sketch, not a family obligation.
Money you give or lend is not shown as returned.
The school trip price stays Rs. 7,500 because no other fare is given.
None of these paths is labelled as the only correct choice.
waitAssumption: If you treat the help as a loan, repayment is not guaranteed unless money actually comes back.

title: An unexpected expense
description: Adapt your plans when something goes wrong.
preview: Something unexpected costs money. How do you adapt a plan that no longer fits?
cubHint: Plans change. The skill is adjusting without ignoring other needs.
situation: You have Rs. 4,000 saved for a goal. A school bag and a bus pass suddenly cost Rs. 2,500.

facts.label: Left if you pay from savings
Other income this month
facts.value: Not included, because none is stated

options.title: Pay from savings and pause the goal
options.summary: Cover the surprise cost and accept a smaller goal balance.
bullets: Pause adding more until you can rebuild.
options.immediate: The bag and bus pass are paid, and the goal drops to Rs. 1,500.
options.future: You avoid new debt. Reaching the original goal will take longer.

snapshot.label: Use savings
snapshot.note: No new borrowing. Rs. 2,500 of the goal has been used.

options.title: Pay the bill and cut other spending
options.summary: Pay the bill, then set aside Rs. 500 by spending less elsewhere.
bullets: Cut about Rs. 500 of other spending and put it back.
End with Rs. 2,000 toward the goal.
options.immediate: The surprise is paid and part of the goal is rebuilt.
options.future: This works only if you can actually cut Rs. 500. That cut is a scenario assumption.

snapshot.label: Adjust the plan
snapshot.note: The Rs. 500 rebuild assumes you can reduce other spending.

options.title: Borrow so the goal stays untouched
options.summary: Keep all Rs. 4,000 saved and borrow the Rs. 2,500.
bullets: Borrow Rs. 2,500 for the bag and bus pass.
options.immediate: The goal balance stays at Rs. 4,000, and a new debt starts.
options.future: You still need a way to repay Rs. 2,500 while continuing the goal.

snapshot.label: Borrow
snapshot.note: Rs. 2,500 remains owed because no repayment schedule is defined.

sixMonthAssumptions: This comparison is a teaching sketch for one unexpected bill.
Borrowed money stays owed because no repayment amount is defined.
Putting Rs. 500 back assumes you can cut other spending by that amount.
None of these paths is labelled as the only correct choice.
waitAssumption: No emergency fund beyond the Rs. 4,000 is included. Borrowing would create a new amount to repay.

title: Saving for a big goal
description: Compare trade-offs when working toward a goal.
preview: A big goal needs time and money. Compare what you give up now to get there later.
cubHint: Waiting can be hard. Compare what you gain and what you postpone.
situation: You have Rs. 5,000 saved toward a Rs. 15,000 trip. If you save Rs. 2,500 a month, the remaining Rs. 10,000 would take about four months. A concert this month costs Rs. 3,000.

options.title: Go to the concert
options.summary: Use Rs. 3,000 of the trip fund for the concert.
bullets: You would then need Rs. 13,000 more.
options.immediate: You attend the concert and the trip fund drops to Rs. 2,000.
options.future: At the assumed Rs. 2,500 a month, Rs. 13,000 would take a little over five months, not four.

snapshot.label: Go to the concert
snapshot.note: No debt. The goal is Rs. 13,000 away after this choice.

options.title: Skip the concert and stay on plan
options.summary: Leave the Rs. 5,000 untouched.
bullets: Do not spend on the concert.
The remaining Rs. 10,000 still matches the four-month example.
options.immediate: The trip plan stays on track, and you miss the concert.
options.future: You give up a present event to keep the later goal closer.

snapshot.label: Stay on plan
snapshot.note: No debt. About Rs. 10,000 is still needed.

options.title: Choose a smaller outing
options.summary: Spend Rs. 1,000 instead of Rs. 3,000.
bullets: Spend Rs. 1,000 on a smaller plan.
The trip then needs Rs. 11,000 more.
options.immediate: You still do something social and keep most of the fund.
options.future: The goal moves back a little. At Rs. 2,500 a month, Rs. 11,000 is still more than four months.

snapshot.label: Smaller outing
snapshot.note: The Rs. 1,000 outing is an example price.

sixMonthAssumptions: This comparison does not invent six months of perfect saving.
Going to the concert lowers today’s balance. Later months are not added unless stated.
A smaller outing at Rs. 1,000 is an example, not a real ticket.
None of these paths is labelled as the only correct choice.
waitAssumption: Saving Rs. 2,500 a month is a scenario assumption, not a guaranteed income. Four months is 10,000 ÷ 2,500.

title: A difficult choice
description: Apply your decision-making skills to a complex situation.
preview: Several needs compete at once. Use what you have practised to think the choice through.
cubHint: Complex choices need the same steps: needs, money, options, and later effects.
situation: You have Rs. 6,000. School materials cost Rs. 2,500 and are due this week. A sibling asks to borrow Rs. 2,000. A game you want costs Rs. 3,000.

options.title: Buy the game and borrow for school
options.summary: Buy the game, lend your sibling Rs. 2,000, and borrow what school still needs.
bullets: Borrow Rs. 1,500 so the Rs. 2,500 school bill can still be paid.
options.immediate: You get the game and help your sibling, but you owe Rs. 1,500 and have Rs. 1,000 left.
options.future: School is paid only because of the loan. You still have to repay Rs. 1,500, and the sibling loan may not come back.

snapshot.label: Game now
snapshot.state: Game bought, sibling lent Rs. 2,000, school borrowed
snapshot.note: You owe Rs. 1,500. The Rs. 2,000 lent to your sibling is not counted as money you still have.

options.title: Pay for school and keep a buffer
options.summary: Cover school, offer a smaller amount to your sibling, and skip the game.
bullets: Offer your sibling Rs. 500 instead of Rs. 2,000.
Keep Rs. 3,000 and skip the game.
options.immediate: School is paid without a new loan, and most of your savings remain.
options.future: You miss the game. Your sibling receives less than they asked for, so you should explain the limit.

snapshot.label: School and buffer
snapshot.state: School paid, small family offer, no game
snapshot.note: No new debt. Rs. 500 shared with your sibling is not assumed to return.

options.title: Give each goal a smaller share
options.summary: Pay school, lend less, and choose a cheaper game example.
bullets: Pay the full Rs. 2,500 school bill.
Spend Rs. 1,500 on a cheaper game example and keep Rs. 1,000.
options.immediate: All three areas get something, and you do not borrow.
options.future: Nobody gets the full original wish. The cheaper game price is an assumption.

snapshot.label: Split three ways
snapshot.state: School paid, partial loan, cheaper game
snapshot.note: No new debt. The Rs. 1,500 game price is an example so the three costs can fit.

sixMonthAssumptions: This comparison is a teaching sketch for one week of competing needs.
Borrowed money stays owed because no repayment plan is defined.
Money lent to your sibling is not shown as repaid.
None of these paths is labelled as the only correct choice.
waitAssumption: Doing all three at the full amounts would cost Rs. 7,500, which is more than your Rs. 6,000. A cheaper game at Rs. 1,500 is only an example.
